newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi denies conflict of interest.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi denies conflict of interest.

text.p: Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Tuesday denied a conflict of interest allegation in an indictment requested against him and condemned leaks to the media of case documents.

A statement issued by Prodi's office said the 57-year-old centre-left leader had not been officially advised he may face trial over alleged irregularities during his chairmanship of giant state holding IRI in 1993.
"One notes, once again, how public opinion has been informed of judicial events and investigative documents in an improper form and before those who are directly interested," it said.

Italian news agencies on Monday broke news that a deputy public prosecutor in Rome, Giuseppa Geremia, had asked for Prodi and the five other members of the IRI board in 1993 to be tried for alleged abuse of office.

The request relates to the sale by IRI in October 1993 of the food company Cirio, best known for its canned tomatoes, to a southern Italian consortium, Fis.Vi. Geremia alleges IRI's board granted the buyer an "unjust advantage" in the sale.

The media reports were detailed but unsourced in keeping with a formula that has marked four years of bombshell investigations by magistrates into alleged malpractice and graft in Italian politics and big business.

They added that Prodi, appointed prime minister in May, faced a separate charge of conflict of interest stemming from a consultancy with the Anglo-Dutch group Unilever, which bought part of Cirio from Fis.Vi shortly after the IRI sale.

"The Prime Minister forcefully rejects such an accusation and points out...that he resigned as a consultant of Unilever Plc and Unilever Nv on May 20, 1993, the date he was appointed chairman of IRI," Tuesday's statement said.
Geremia's trial request must go before an examining judge, who can decide to indict the suspects, drop the case or order further investigations.
Prodi, questioned in the investigation last March, said on Monday that the sale was in order and that he was confident that Italy's judicial system would clear him.
He was chairman of IRI for most of the 1980s and was brought back for a further year from May 1993 when the then-incument, Franco Nobili, was himself arrested in a corruption inquiry.
Support for Prodi has come from across most of the political spectrum, with only isolated calls for his resignation.

Among those springing to his defence was media mogul and conservative former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, advised when in office in 1994 that he was under investigation for alleged bribery and now a defendant in two separate trials.
Prodi and Berlusconi, leader of the main centre-right opposition, share the same defence lawyer, Giuseppe De Luca.

Prodi's problems returned the spotlight to whether the time has come to find a way out of the judicial assault that has overshadowed Italian affairs since 1992 and establish a clearer division of powers between politics and the judiciary.

"Can a country seek normality when, though in different ways and for different alleged offences, the prime minister, the leader of the biggest party and the leader of the opposition all stand accused of something?" Il Messaggero newspaper asked.

Massimo D'Alema, whose Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest in government and in parliament, is under investigation over past alleged irregular financial links between the party and Italian cooperatives.
